❯ Write a 400-word essay about the colour blue. Plain prose, no headings.

● Blue is the colour that arrives late. Ancient languages often lacked a word for it, and Homer famously described the
  sea as wine-dark rather than blue. Blue pigments were rare in nature and expensive to produce, so for much of human
  history blue was something people saw in the sky and the water but could not easily hold in their hands. When lapis
  lazuli was ground into ultramarine, it cost more than gold, and Renaissance painters reserved it for the robes of the
  Virgin Mary, a colour so precious it became a form of devotion.

  That scarcity gave blue a strange double life. It is the most common answer when people are asked their favourite
  colour, yet it is one of the rarest colours in living things. Blue flowers are uncommon, blue animals are mostly
  tricks of light rather than pigment, and blue food looks faintly wrong on a plate. The blue of a jay's feather or a
  morpho butterfly's wing is structural, made by microscopic ridges that scatter light, and it vanishes if the feather
  is crushed. Blue, in other words, is often not a substance but an event.

  Perhaps that is why it carries so much feeling. We speak of feeling blue, of blue notes bent slightly flat in a jazz
  solo, of the blues themselves, a whole musical tradition built on longing. Blue is the colour of distance. Hills far
  away turn blue because the air between us and them scatters short wavelengths, and so blue became the colour of things
  we cannot reach: the horizon, the deep sea, the past. Rebecca Solnit called it the blue of distance, the colour of
  where you are not.

  And yet blue is also the colour of calm and trust. Banks, hospitals, and uniforms lean on it because it suggests
  steadiness and competence. A clear blue sky promises a good day. The pale blue of a swimming pool or a summer morning
  feels like an open invitation. Blue can be cold, but it is rarely hostile. It cools a room without emptying it.

  Seen from space, our planet is blue, mostly water and atmosphere wrapped around rock. Carl Sagan's pale blue dot
  reminded us how small and fragile that is. Blue is the colour of everything vast we live inside of and everything
  faraway we ache toward. It is the colour of the sky above and the sea below, and of the thin line where they meet.
